Most recently, I decide to go back with friends and my parents after seeing the kitchen nightmares episode and was happy to see a good number of tables full on a Wednesday evening. As so many dishes were passed around our table and shared I'll admit nothing was exciting but all that I tasted was good. The Fishtown Chowder was mild but really tasty at the same time. I would definitely return for that on a cold night. The spinach salad with walnuts was standard but good and the sheppards pie was good but bland. Salt and Pepper were not offered on the table but instead, shakers with some sort of their own special seasonings which seemed the color of old bay. Not knowing what exactly that was made it less enticing to use apprently, since no one at our table did. The potatoes and minced lamb was really tasty but that's all there was. Someone at the table longed for peas and onions or something, anything to liven it up. The crab cakes were very good and the potato encrusted salmon sounded more interesting than the reality of it being just hashbrown shredded potato atop the salmon. It was good though, dont get me wrong, just not as encrustastic. Dessert was a shared sweet potato cheese cake which was light and delicous and then there was their version of home made butter cake. It's not butter cake in any sense that I grew up with but it was very good nonetheless. The menu is conservative but tasty and with plenty of low priced options. I hope this neighborhood establishment which has been transformed sticks around a long time.

text: I had an interesting experience at this place... My boyfriend and I had been out drinking and were walking down Bourbon Street on the way back to our hotel. We were both pretty inebriated and having a great time. We pass by the Old Opera House (by the way, don't let the name fool you, this place is just another dumpy Bourbon street bar populated by drunk frat boys), and the lovely hostess in front of the bar starts talking to us. She calls us a cute couple, chats with us for a little while, and ends up offering us shots out of test tubes (don't ask). We're not the kind to refuse a free drink, so my boyfriend and I indulge in "a few" shots (crappy booze, by the way). Ten minutes of friendly conversation and a few shots later, our lovely hostess becomes serious, and flatly tells us that we owe her $48. As we realize, we are also surrounded at this point by two big bouncers. WTF? She offered us the shots, never said they were for sale, never told us a price or gave us any indication that we'd get charged for them. By that time, she wasn't the friendly person who'd lured us in anymore... We tried to argue with her and her bouncer friends, who decided simply to threaten to call the police: "You pay or go to jail". Are you effin' kidding me? Pay or go to jail, for drinks that we never ordered? We ended up going in the back, talking to the manager (who blended right in in the crowd of dimwitted frat boys), and after a few minutes of argument ended up paying $24 for the shots of crappy booze that we never ordered but were simply put in our hands. Lesson learned: Bourbon street is a tourist trap. Don't count on the generosity of strangers there: people are after your money, and will take advantage of your drunkenness to squeeze it out of you. Just pathetic.

text: Went here last night with two friends. I heard about this place the last time I was in Nashville and knew that I wanted to come check it out during this trip. I would feel more comfortable giving it a higher rating if I didn't feel like Whiskey Kitchen is suffering from an identity crisis. The decor of the place feels like it's cool, hip, high-end yet approachable. I loved the light fixtures and the dark wall treatment. What I really didn't like was the plastic ketchup, mustard, assorted condiment "tool box" on top of every table. Plastic containers? really? I get that burgers are popular... but why eschew glass bottles for plastic? Am I at a picnic or a nice, cool cocktail bar, or the bbq shack down the street? The whole tool box, condiment corral is big and takes up a lot of space. It really doesn't jive with the rest of the decor. On to the positives! The drinks! Since it is the WHISKEY Kitchen, I ordered one of their signature whiskey drinks called the Amber. It was divine. wow. Talk about packing a punch! Once my mouth got used to a few sips, I only tasted the strawberries and cinnamon. So good. Highly recommend it. My friend had the tuna and it was great. I had the grilled chicken skewers served with fries and aioli. The chicken was a little bland, but the fries and aioli were deliciously perfect. For dessert, we shared their flour-less chocolate cake served with raspberries and blueberries. The waitress had me at flour-less. It was close-your-eyes worthy good. Oh, if you drive, they have additional parking across the street.

text: To get straight to the point, I would not go back to this place for any reason. I was looking for Italian in the area, still am looking for a reasonably priced place with good Italian food, but alas. The atmosphere was alright, but some of the decor is questionable. The sign outside is comical with it's Mr. Rogers Neighborhood kind of font, yet the inside has chandeliers and white linen tablecloths. There was a piano player in the bar area, but to tell you the truth, I had to laugh then groan because I never thought I would hear Creed played seriously for an audience on a lounge piano. But I digress...on to the food. My friend and I split our meal, based on the suggestion of another reviewer for the $2 split charge, which was good because this placed is definitely overpriced for the quality. The quantity was just fine for us as it also came with a salad, we just ordered an extra salad. My mixed greens with balsamic vinaigrette was very boring and they only gave me one sliced tomato. The vinaigrette was bland and I have never had to do this before, but I had to add some sugar to my salad to give the balsamic some flavor. My friend's Caesar salad was also a bit bland and the croutons were quite stale and funny tasting. The dish we had was linguine with mussels in a red sauce. The mussels, to give credit, were cooked fine and tasted good. The sauce on the pasta was a bit cloudy/milky looking...which I was concerned about because it did not look fresh or home made. It looked like something out of a Chef Boyardee can, which is something I have chosen not to eat since I was a child. I could tell at first bite the sodium content was really high, so I was very disappointed in the quality of the sauce and would bet it was probably canned. The pasta was a tad overcooked too, so it really was a lot like eating spaghettios. :/ We did not bother having any of the desserts they showed us on the dessert tray, not only because they looked old and congealed (I know, it's been on display, but still - presentation!) but after all that, we didn't trust them to deliver the taste we were expecting. The server was matter of fact, but knew her stuff and we had no complaints with service. They had a runner deliver all the food and she followed with grated pepper and Parmesan cheese, although I didn't care, some might find this, being offered pepper on your salad after you've eaten a quarter of it already. Bottom line: The prices are not worth the quality of food. Our meal was about $16 plus the split charge and the salad ($5, which was the only reasonably priced item on the menu). All the other entrees were priced from $15 to $29. I might have gotten a different result with another entree, but I was so unimpressed that I will not bother to try them out again. If you are reading this and you ARE looking for excellent Italian regardless of price, I highly recommend Moonstruck in Rockledge/Fox Chase. They are also pricey, but their food is good enough that it is worth the money.

text: Having Rolling Hill Park as an asset makes me so happy to be a resident of Lower Merion Township. This property could have easily been sold off to developers for millions upon millions of dollars, but the township transformed this historic property that changed hands many times in to a world class park. I've been exploring Rolling Hill Park ever since the summer of 1996, and it came along way since then. Rolling Hill Park was bought from the Pew family in 1995, and transformed in to the park that we see today. Let me give you a brief overview of the park. The first mill was built in 1764, and transformed in to a huge mill at the lower end of the park along Mill Creek. Throughout the lower portion of the park, you will find 4 stone ruins of the mill workers dormitories. On the upper portion of the park, to your left hand side, you will see a stone building in ruins and a concrete silo. These along with a pig stable down a little further are what remain of the old farm days of the property. The upper portion changes hands a few times from a farm to a residence and then was bought by the Pew Family (founders of Sun Oil Company, you may know it as Sunoco) after the Stock Market crashed in 1929. The highlight of the property was a large modern mansion that was built by the last owner. The Pews built a lot on the upper portion, including a large pool. This pool was filled in, and the pool house ruins were there to explore in 1996. Now in it's place is a set of bathrooms built in the same stone style, and you can still see the outline of the pool in stone. If you walk straight down the main path, to the large clearing you will see a lot of steps and stone blocks. This is the remains of the old garden that was in front of the mansion. The old mansion was being dismantled in 1958 when it burnt down, and none of it remains today. Now back to the park. The park is beautiful. You have what I believe is over 100 acres to explore including all the old ruins, many paths, and very interesting historic relics from the early 19th and 20th century still around. You can go down to Mill Creek and sift through the water to find tiny broken pieces of pottery from the days of the mill workers. Every time I head to Rolling Hill Park, I always find something interesting and brand new to me. You have more than enough room go explore and never see someone else your entire time, which is why Rolling Hill Park is so special to have.
